questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

# Laptop Dialer — System Design

Desktop app (Windows + macOS) that calls Indian mobile numbers over the internet.

> Working name only. Avoid shipping as "Paytm…" — trademark risk.

## 1. Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app | **Wails v2** (Go + React/TS UI) | One Go codebase, native installers for Win/Mac, ~10–30 MB vs Electron ~150 MB |
| Call audio | **Twilio Voice JS SDK** in the app's webview (WebRTC) | Audio goes laptop ↔ Twilio directly. No media server to run |
| Backend API | **Go on Vercel Functions** (Go runtime, `api/*.go`) | Free Hobby tier, git-push deploy |
| Database | **Neon** (serverless Postgres) | Free tier, `pgx` driver |
| Telephony | **Twilio trial** (MVP) → Indian licensed provider (prod) | See §6 |

The backend never carries audio. It only issues tokens, gives Twilio its call instructions, and logs calls.

## 2. Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────── Laptop ────────────────────────────┐
│  Wails app                                                     │
│   ├─ Go side: login, secure token storage (OS keychain)        │
│   └─ UI (React): dialer, call timer, history                   │
│        └─ Twilio Voice SDK ── WebRTC audio ──────────┐         │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┘
               │ HTTPS (JWT)                           │
┌──────────────▼──────────────┐                ┌───────▼────────┐
│  Vercel (Go functions)      │◄── webhooks ───│    Twilio      │
│   /api/login                │── TwiML ──────►│   (PSTN gw)    │
│   /api/token                │                └───────┬────────┘
│   /api/voice   (TwiML)      │                        │ PSTN
│   /api/status  (callback)   │                ┌───────▼────────┐
│   /api/calls   (history)    │                │ Indian mobile  │
└──────────────┬──────────────┘                │  +91XXXXXXXXXX │
               │ pgx (TLS)                     └────────────────┘
┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Neon Postgres              │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

## 3. Call flow

```
App                  Vercel API              Twilio               Mobile
 │ POST /api/login ──►│ check bcrypt → JWT    │                     │
 │◄── JWT ────────────│                       │                     │
 │ GET /api/token ───►│ sign Access Token     │                     │
 │◄── twilio token ───│ (Voice grant, 1h TTL) │                     │
 │ Device.connect({To:"+91…"}) ─────────────► │                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/voice ───│ (signed webhook)    │
 │                    │ verify signature,     │                     │
 │                    │ validate +91 number,  │                     │
 │                    │ insert call row       │                     │
 │                    │── <Dial><Number> ────►│── ring ────────────►│
 │◄═════════════════ WebRTC audio ═══════════►│◄═══ voice ═════════►│
 │ hangup ───────────────────────────────────►│                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/status ──│ (duration, price)   │
 │                    │ update call row       │                     │
 │ GET /api/calls ───►│ history               │                     │
```

## 4. API

| Route | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/signup` | none | email + password → user (bcrypt) |
| `POST /api/login` | none | → app JWT (HS256, 7d) |
| `GET /api/token` | app JWT | → Twilio Access Token, identity = user id |
| `POST /api/voice` | Twilio signature | Returns TwiML `<Dial callerId=…><Number>+91…</Number></Dial>` |
| `POST /api/status` | Twilio signature | Final status, duration, price → `calls` |
| `GET /api/calls` | app JWT | User's last 50 calls |

Rules for `/api/voice`:
- Reject a request unless `X-Twilio-Signature` is valid. This stops strangers from using your account to place calls.
- `To` must match `^\+91[6-9]\d{9}$` (Indian mobile). Reject everything else so nobody can dial premium or international numbers.
- Per-user daily minute cap (MVP: 20 min), checked against `calls`.

## 5. Database (Neon)

```sql
create table users (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text unique not null,
  password_hash text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table calls (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  call_sid    text unique not null,
  to_number   text not null,
  status      text not null default 'initiated',
  duration_s  int  not null default 0,
  price       numeric(10,4),
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  ended_at    timestamptz
);
create index on calls (user_id, created_at desc);
```

## 6. India: provider and compliance

- **MVP (Twilio trial):** free trial credit. You can only call **verified** numbers (verify your test mobiles by OTP in the Twilio console). Every call starts with a trial announcement. Turn on India in *Voice → Geo Permissions*. Caller ID shows your Twilio number, which is not Indian. That's fine for testing.
- **Production:** under Indian telecom rules, internet-to-phone calling inside India must go through a licensed operator. Before launch, move to an Indian licensed cloud-telephony provider (e.g. Exotel, Plivo India, Airtel IQ, Tata Tele). These need business KYC. Keep all telephony code in `internal/telephony` so the switch only touches that package.
- Verify current rules with the provider during KYC. This section is not legal advice.

## 7. Repo layout

```
/
├── api/                  # Vercel Go functions (one Handler per file)
│   ├── login.go  signup.go  token.go  voice.go  status.go  calls.go
├── internal/
│   ├── db/               # pgx pool (Neon)
│   ├── auth/             # JWT + bcrypt
│   └── telephony/        # Twilio: token, TwiML, signature check
├── desktop/              # Wails app
│   ├── main.go  app.go   # Go side: login, keychain
│   └── frontend/         # React + TS + @twilio/voice-sdk
├── go.mod
└── DESIGN.md
```

## 8. Config (Vercel env vars)

```
DATABASE_URL            Neon pooled connection string
JWT_SECRET              random 32+ bytes
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN       used to verify webhooks
TWILIO_API_KEY_SID      used to sign access tokens
TWILIO_API_KEY_SECRET
TWILIO_TWIML_APP_SID    TwiML App → Voice URL = https://<app>.vercel.app/api/voice
TWILIO_CALLER_ID        your Twilio number
```

Secrets stay in Vercel only. The desktop app holds just the API base URL and the user's JWT, stored in the OS keychain.

## 9. Build order

0. **Spike (do first):** Wails app + Twilio SDK placing one call. This proves WebRTC and the microphone work in WebView2 (Windows) and WKWebView (macOS). The macOS build needs `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`. **If the mic or WebRTC fails in WKWebView, switch the desktop app to Electron.** The React UI carries over unchanged.
1. Neon schema + `internal/db`.
2. `signup` / `login` / `token`.
3. `voice` + `status` with signature checks, number validation, daily cap.
4. Desktop: login screen, dialer, call timer, history.
5. Package: `wails build` → `.exe` (Windows), `.app`/`.dmg` (macOS; signing and notarization needed for distribution).

## 10. Known limits

- Vercel Hobby is **non-commercial only**. Move to Pro before charging users.
- The Vercel Go runtime is the least mature Vercel runtime. Keep handlers plain `net/http` so they could move to any host.
- Twilio trial can only call verified numbers. Fine for an MVP with 10–20 test calls, not for real users.
- MVP skips: wallet/billing, contacts, call recording, incoming calls. Add once outbound works.

Desktop app (Windows + macOS) that calls Indian mobile numbers over the internet.

> Working name only. Avoid shipping as "Paytm…" — trademark risk.

## 1. Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app | **Wails v2** (Go + React/TS UI) | One Go codebase, native installers for Win/Mac, ~10–30 MB vs Electron ~150 MB |
| Call audio | **Twilio Voice JS SDK** in the app's webview (WebRTC) | Audio goes laptop ↔ Twilio directly. No media server to run |
| Backend API | **Go on Vercel Functions** (Go runtime, `api/*.go`) | Free Hobby tier, git-push deploy |
| Database | **Neon** (serverless Postgres) | Free tier, `pgx` driver |
| Telephony | **Twilio trial** (MVP) → Indian licensed provider (prod) | See §6 |

The backend never carries audio. It only issues tokens, gives Twilio its call instructions, and logs calls.

## 2. Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────── Laptop ────────────────────────────┐
│  Wails app                                                     │
│   ├─ Go side: login, secure token storage (OS keychain)        │
│   └─ UI (React): dialer, call timer, history                   │
│        └─ Twilio Voice SDK ── WebRTC audio ──────────┐         │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┘

┌──────────────▼──────────────┐                ┌───────▼────────┐
│  Vercel (Go functions)      │◄── webhooks ───│    Twilio      │
│   /api/login                │── TwiML ──────►│   (PSTN gw)    │
│   /api/token                │                └───────┬────────┘
│   /api/voice   (TwiML)      │                        │ PSTN
│   /api/status  (callback)   │                ┌───────▼────────┐
│   /api/calls   (history)    │                │ Indian mobile  │
└──────────────┬──────────────┘                │  +91XXXXXXXXXX │
               │ pgx (TLS)                     └────────────────┘
┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Neon Postgres              │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

## 3. Call flow

```
App                  Vercel API              Twilio               Mobile
 │ POST /api/login ──►│ check bcrypt → JWT    │                     │
 │◄── JWT ────────────│                       │                     │
 │ GET /api/token ───►│ sign Access Token     │                     │
 │◄── twilio token ───│ (Voice grant, 1h TTL) │                     │
 │ Device.connect({To:"+91…"}) ─────────────► │                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/voice ───│ (signed webhook)    │
 │                    │ verify signature,     │                     │
 │                    │ validate +91 number,  │                     │
 │                    │ insert call row       │                     │
 │                    │── <Dial><Number> ────►│── ring ────────────►│

 │ hangup ───────────────────────────────────►│                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/status ──│ (duration, price)   │
 │                    │ update call row       │                     │
 │ GET /api/calls ───►│ history               │                     │
```

| Route | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/signup` | none | email + password → user (bcrypt) |
| `POST /api/login` | none | → app JWT (HS256, 7d) |
| `GET /api/token` | app JWT | → Twilio Access Token, identity = user id |
| `POST /api/voice` | Twilio signature | Returns TwiML `<Dial callerId=…><Number>+91…</Number></Dial>` |
| `POST /api/status` | Twilio signature | Final status, duration, price → `calls` |
| `GET /api/calls` | app JWT | User's last 50 calls |

- Reject a request unless `X-Twilio-Signature` is valid. This stops strangers from using your account to place calls.
- `To` must match `^\+91[6-9]\d{9}$` (Indian mobile). Reject everything else so nobody can dial premium or international numbers.
- Per-user daily minute cap (MVP: 20 min), checked against `calls`.

## 5. Database (Neon)

```sql
create table users (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text unique not null,
  password_hash text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table calls (

Keep all telephony code in `internal/telephony` so the switch only touches that package.

/

│   ├── login.go  signup.go  token.go  voice.go  status.go  calls.go

├── go.mod

```

JWT_SECRET              random 32+ bytes
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN       used to verify webhooks
TWILIO_API_KEY_SID      used to sign access tokens
TWILIO_API_KEY_SECRET

Yes. Your SIM can place the calls, and most Indian plans include unlimited calling, so calls cost nothing extra. Your phone has to be on and nearby (same Wi‑Fi or Bluetooth). The deciding question is where the call audio should play.

**Option A: audio on the laptop, using what's built in (no code)**
- Windows: Microsoft **Phone Link** with an Android phone or iPhone. You dial on the PC and talk through the PC mic and speaker over Bluetooth.
- Mac: **iPhone Continuity** ("Calls from iPhone"). Mac doesn't offer this for Android phones.
- This already does the job. Building it yourself means writing Bluetooth headset-protocol code, which is hard and fragile.

**Option B: laptop is the dialer, audio stays on the phone (buildable, free)**
- The laptop app handles the dial pad, contacts, history and click-to-call.
- A small **Android helper app** gets "dial +91…" from the laptop and places a normal SIM call.
- You talk on the phone, or on earphones connected to the phone.
- The laptop can't receive the call audio over the internet. Since Android 10, apps aren't allowed to capture call audio.
- Stack stays close to the design: Go on Vercel and Neon pass dial commands and store history. Android helper in Kotlin. Phone needs internet. Android only; iPhone doesn't allow apps to place calls automatically.

**Avoid:** "GSM gateway" or "SIM box" setups that route internet calls out through SIM cards. They're **illegal in India**.

**Recommendation:**
- For your own personal use: Option A, nothing to build.
- To build a product or add features like CRM, logs or auto-dialing: Option B.

Do you need the voice on the laptop, or is dialing from the laptop and talking on the phone fine? And are your phones Android or iPhone?

# Laptop Dialer — System Design

Desktop app (Windows + macOS) that dials Indian numbers. The user picks one of two modes per call:

| Mode | Who places the call | Where the voice is | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **My phone (SIM)** | User's own Android phone, normal SIM call | On the phone (handset or earphones) | Free on unlimited plans |
| **Internet (Twilio)** | Twilio, over the internet | On the laptop (mic + speakers) | Free trial credit (MVP) |

> Working name only. Avoid shipping as "Paytm…" — trademark risk.

## 1. Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app | **Wails v2** (Go + React/TS UI) | One Go codebase, native Win/Mac installers, small binary |
| Android helper | **Kotlin**, minimal app | Receives dial commands, places SIM calls, reports results |
| Push to phone | **Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)** | Free. Reaches the phone even when the helper app is in the background |
| Internet audio | **Twilio Voice JS SDK** in the desktop webview | Audio goes laptop ↔ Twilio directly |
| Backend API | **Go on Vercel Functions** (`api/*.go`) | Free Hobby tier, git-push deploy |
| Database | **Neon** (serverless Postgres) | Free tier, `pgx` driver |

The backend never carries audio. It only relays commands, issues tokens and stores call logs.

## 2. Architecture

```
┌───────────── Laptop (Wails app) ─────────────┐
│  Dialer UI  [ My phone | Internet ] toggle   │
│   └─ Twilio Voice SDK (Internet mode only) ══╪══ WebRTC ══╗
└───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘            ║
                │ HTTPS + JWT                                ║
┌───────────────▼──────────────┐   webhooks   ┌─────────────▼──┐
│  Vercel (Go functions)       │◄────────────►│    Twilio      │
│  /api/login /api/signup      │              └─────────┬──────┘
│  /api/devices  /api/dial     │                        │ PSTN
│  /api/calls  /api/calls/:id  │                        ▼
│  /api/token /api/voice       │                 Indian number
│  /api/status                 │                        ▲
└──────┬────────────────┬──────┘                        │ SIM call
       │ pgx            │ FCM push                      │
┌──────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼─────────────────────────┐     │
│ Neon        │  │ Android helper (user's phone)  │─────┘
│ Postgres    │  │ places call, reports status    │
└─────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘
```

## 3. Flows

### 3a. My phone (SIM) mode

```
Laptop              Vercel API             FCM          Android helper        Callee
 │ POST /api/dial ─►│ insert call          │                │                    │
 │ {to, mode:sim}   │ (status=queued)      │                │                    │
 │                  │── push {callId,to} ─►│── deliver ────►│                    │
 │◄── {callId} ─────│                      │                │ placeCall(to) ────►│ rings
 │                  │◄── POST /api/calls/:id {status:dialing} ─┤                    │
 │ poll every 2s    │                      │                │   … talking on phone …
 │ GET /api/calls/:id                      │                │ call ends          │
 │                  │◄── POST /api/calls/:id {status:ended, duration_s} ─┤        │
 │◄── ended, 3m12s ─│                      │                │                    │
```

- Pairing: the user signs in to the Android helper with the same email and password. The helper then registers its FCM token through `POST /api/devices`.
- Placing the call: `TelecomManager.placeCall()` with the `CALL_PHONE` permission. The phone's normal in-call screen opens and the voice stays on the phone.
- Duration: after the call ends, read the newest outgoing entry in `CallLog` (`READ_CALL_LOG`). That gives the real talk time.
- Hanging up: done on the phone. Laptop-side hangup is skipped in the MVP (it needs `ANSWER_PHONE_CALLS` and `TelecomManager.endCall()`, which is deprecated).

### 3b. Internet (Twilio) mode

```
Laptop                Vercel API              Twilio              Callee
 │ GET /api/token ───►│ Access Token (1h)     │                     │
 │ Device.connect({To}) ─────────────────────►│                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/voice ───│ signed webhook      │
 │                    │ verify, validate, cap │                     │
 │                    │ insert call row       │                     │
 │                    │── <Dial><Number> ────►│── ring ────────────►│
 │◄════════════ WebRTC audio ════════════════►│◄═══ voice ═════════►│
 │                    │◄── POST /api/status ──│ duration, price     │
```

## 4. API

| Route | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/signup` | none | email + password → user (bcrypt) |
| `POST /api/login` | none | → JWT (HS256, 7 days) |
| `POST /api/devices` | JWT | Android helper registers or refreshes its FCM token |
| `POST /api/dial` | JWT | SIM mode: create call row, push to the user's device, return `callId` |
| `GET /api/calls/:id` | JWT | Status of one call (laptop polls this) |
| `POST /api/calls/:id` | JWT (device) | Android helper reports `dialing` / `ended` / `failed` + `duration_s` |
| `GET /api/calls` | JWT | Last 50 calls, both modes |
| `GET /api/token` | JWT | Twilio Access Token, identity = user id |
| `POST /api/voice` | Twilio signature | TwiML `<Dial callerId=…><Number>+91…</Number></Dial>` |
| `POST /api/status` | Twilio signature | Final Twilio status, duration, price |

Validation (both modes):
- `to` must match `^\+91\d{10}$`.
- Twilio webhooks are rejected unless `X-Twilio-Signature` is valid. Without that check, anyone who finds the URL could place calls on your account.
- Twilio mode: per-user daily cap (MVP: 20 min) so the trial credit isn't drained.
- Calls can only be read or updated by their owner (`user_id` check on every `:id` route).

## 5. Database (Neon)

```sql
create table users (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text unique not null,
  password_hash text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table devices (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  fcm_token   text unique not null,
  updated_at  timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table calls (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  mode        text not null check (mode in ('sim','twilio')),
  to_number   text not null,
  status      text not null default 'queued',
  duration_s  int  not null default 0,
  call_sid    text unique,            -- twilio only
  price       numeric(10,4),          -- twilio only
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  ended_at    timestamptz
);
create index on calls (user_id, created_at desc);
```

MVP: one device per user. The newest `devices` row wins.

## 6. India and compliance

- **SIM mode:** a normal mobile call from the user's own SIM. No telecom licence issue.
- **Twilio mode (MVP):** trial only calls **verified** numbers (verify test mobiles by OTP in the Twilio console), plays a trial announcement, and shows a non-Indian caller ID. Turn on India in *Voice → Geo Permissions*. Before real users, internet-to-phone calling inside India must move to an Indian licensed provider (Exotel, Plivo India, Airtel IQ, Tata Tele; business KYC needed). Twilio code lives only in `internal/telephony`.
- **Never** route internet calls out through SIM cards (GSM gateway or SIM box). It's illegal in India. SIM mode is different: only the phone's owner places calls, one at a time, from their own phone.
- Not legal advice. Confirm with the provider during KYC.

## 7. Repo layout

```
/
├── api/                     # Vercel Go functions
│   ├── signup.go login.go devices.go dial.go calls.go
│   └── token.go voice.go status.go
├── internal/
│   ├── db/                  # pgx pool (Neon)
│   ├── auth/                # JWT + bcrypt
│   ├── push/                # FCM HTTP v1 sender
│   └── telephony/           # Twilio: token, TwiML, signature check
├── desktop/                 # Wails app (Go + React/TS + @twilio/voice-sdk)
├── android/                 # Kotlin helper app
├── go.mod
└── DESIGN.md
```

## 8. Config

Vercel env vars:
```
DATABASE_URL              Neon pooled connection string
JWT_SECRET                random 32+ bytes
FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON  Firebase service account (for sending pushes)
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN         used to verify webhooks
TWILIO_API_KEY_SID        used to sign access tokens
TWILIO_API_KEY_SECRET
TWILIO_TWIML_APP_SID      TwiML App Voice URL = https://<app>.vercel.app/api/voice
TWILIO_CALLER_ID
```
Desktop app stores only the API URL and the user's JWT (in the OS keychain). The Android app ships `google-services.json` plus the API URL.

## 9. Build order

0. **Spikes (do first, each about half a day):**
   - a. Android: FCM message arrives while the app is in the background → `placeCall()` dials. Test on 2–3 phone brands. Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones aggressively kill background apps, so the user may need to turn off battery optimisation for the helper.
   - b. Wails + Twilio SDK: one call each on Windows (WebView2) and macOS (WKWebView, needs `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`). **If the mic or WebRTC fails in WKWebView, switch the desktop app to Electron.** The React UI carries over unchanged.
1. Neon schema + `internal/db` + `internal/auth` + signup/login.
2. SIM mode end to end: `devices`, `dial`, `calls/:id`, Android helper, laptop dial screen + polling.
3. Twilio mode: `token`, `voice`, `status`, mode toggle in the UI.
4. History screen.
5. Packaging: `wails build` → `.exe` / `.app`. Android APK installed directly on the phone (sideloaded).

## 10. Known limits

- **Android only for SIM mode.** iPhone apps can't place calls without the user tapping.
- **Not on the Play Store yet.** Google restricts `READ_CALL_LOG` to default dialer apps, so the MVP helper is installed directly as an APK. For the Play Store, drop call-log reading (estimate duration from call-state changes) or become the phone's default dialer app.
- The phone needs internet (Wi‑Fi or mobile data) to receive dial commands.
- The laptop learns call status by polling every 2s. Move to WebSockets if that becomes too slow or costly.
- Vercel Hobby is **non-commercial only**. Move to Pro before charging users.
- The Vercel Go runtime is the least mature Vercel runtime. Handlers are plain `net/http` so they can move hosts.
- MVP skips: hangup from the laptop, contacts, recording, incoming calls, multiple devices per user.

 │                  │◄── POST /api/calls/:id {status:ended, duration_s} ─┤        │
 │◄── ended, 3m12s ─│                      │                │                    │

- Placing the call: `TelecomManager.placeCall()` with the `CALL_PHONE` permission. The phone's normal in-call screen opens and the voice stays on the phone.

### 3b. Internet (Twilio) mode

```
Laptop                Vercel API              Twilio              Callee
 │ GET /api/token ───►│ Access Token (1h)     │                     │
 │ Device.connect({To}) ─────────────────────►│                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/voice ───│ signed webhook      │
 │                    │ verify, validate, cap │                     │
 │                    │ insert call row       │                     │
 │                    │── <Dial><Number> ────►│── ring ────────────►│
 │◄════════════ WebRTC audio ════════════════►│◄═══ voice ═════════►│

```

| Route | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|

| `POST /api/login` | none | → JWT (HS256, 7 days) |
| `POST /api/devices` | JWT | Android helper registers or refreshes its FCM token |
| `POST /api/dial` | JWT | SIM mode: create call row, push to the user's device, return `callId` |
| `GET /api/calls/:id` | JWT | Status of one call (laptop polls this) |

| `GET /api/calls` | JWT | Last 50 calls, both modes |
| `GET /api/token` | JWT | Twilio Access Token, identity = user id |
| `POST /api/voice` | Twilio signature | TwiML `<Dial callerId=…><Number>+91…</Number></Dial>` |
| `POST /api/status` | Twilio signature | Final Twilio status, duration, price |

- `to` must match `^\+91\d{10}$`.
- Twilio webhooks are rejected unless `X-Twilio-Signature` is valid. Without that check, anyone who finds the URL could place calls on your account.
- Twilio mode: per-user daily cap (MVP: 20 min) so the trial credit isn't drained.
- Calls can only be read or updated by their owner (`user_id` check on every `:id` route).

## 5. Database (Neon)

```sql
create table users (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text unique not null,
  password_hash text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table devices (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  fcm_token   text unique not null,
  updated_at  timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table calls (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  mode        text not null check (mode in ('sim','twilio')),
  to_number   text not null,
  status      text not null default 'queued',
  duration_s  int  not null default 0,
  call_sid    text unique,            -- twilio only
  price       numeric(10,4),          -- twilio only
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  ended_at    timestamptz
);

```

## 6. India and compliance

- **SIM mode:** a normal mobile call from the user's own SIM. No telecom licence issue.
- **Twilio mode (MVP):** trial only calls **verified** numbers (verify test mobiles by OTP in the Twilio console), plays a trial announcement, and shows a non-Indian caller ID. Turn on India in *Voice → Geo Permissions*. Before real users, internet-to-phone calling inside India must move to an Indian licensed provider (Exotel, Plivo India, Airtel IQ, Tata Tele; business KYC needed). - Not legal advice. Confirm with the provider during KYC.

## 7. Repo layout

```
/
├── api/                     # Vercel Go functions
│   ├── signup.go login.go devices.go dial.go calls.go
│   └── token.go voice.go status.go
├── internal/
│   ├── db/                  # pgx pool (Neon)
│   ├── auth/                # JWT + bcrypt
│   ├── push/                # FCM HTTP v1 sender
│   └── telephony/           # Twilio: token, TwiML, signature check
├── desktop/                 # Wails app (Go + React/TS + @twilio/voice-sdk)
├── android/                 # Kotlin helper app
├── go.mod
└── DESIGN.md
```

## 8. Config

Vercel env vars:
```
DATABASE_URL              Neon pooled connection string
JWT_SECRET                random 32+ bytes
FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON  Firebase service account (for sending pushes)
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN         used to verify webhooks
TWILIO_API_KEY_SID        used to sign access tokens
TWILIO_API_KEY_SECRET
TWILIO_TWIML_APP_SID      TwiML App Voice URL = https://<app>.vercel.app/api/voice
TWILIO_CALLER_ID
```
Desktop app stores only the API URL and the user's JWT (in the OS keychain). The Android app ships `google-services.json` plus the API URL.

## 9. Build order

0. **Spikes (do first, each about half a day):**
   - a. Android: FCM message arrives while the app is in the background → `placeCall()` dials. Test on 2–3 phone brands. Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones aggressively kill background apps, so the user may need to turn off battery optimisation for the helper.

1. Neon schema + `internal/db` + `internal/auth` + signup/login.
2. SIM mode end to end: `devices`, `dial`, `calls/:id`, Android helper, laptop dial screen + polling.
3. Twilio mode: `token`, `voice`, `status`, mode toggle in the UI.
4. History screen.
5. Packaging: `wails build` → `.exe` / `.app`. Android APK installed directly on the phone (sideloaded).

## 10. Known limits

- **Android only for SIM mode.** iPhone apps can't place calls without the user tapping.
- **Not on the Play Store yet.** Google restricts `READ_CALL_LOG` to default dialer apps, so the MVP helper is installed directly as an APK. For the Play Store, drop call-log reading (estimate duration from call-state changes) or become the phone's default dialer app.

- Vercel Hobby is **non-commercial only**. Move to Pro before charging users.

| Mode | Who places the call | Where the voice is | Cost |

| **My phone (SIM)** | User's own Android phone, normal SIM call | On the phone (handset or earphones) | Free on unlimited plans |
| **Internet (Twilio)** | Twilio, over the internet | On the laptop (mic + speakers) | Free trial credit (MVP) |

## 1. Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |

| Push to phone | **Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)** | Free. Reaches the phone even when the helper app is in the background |

| Backend API | **Go on Vercel Functions** (`api/*.go`) | Free Hobby tier, git-push deploy |

# Laptop Dialer — System Design

Desktop app (Windows + macOS) that calls Indian mobile numbers over the internet.

> Working name only. Avoid shipping as "Paytm…" — trademark risk.

## 1. Stack

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app | **Wails v2** (Go + React/TS UI) | One Go codebase, native installers for Win/Mac, ~10–30 MB vs Electron ~150 MB |
| Call audio | **Twilio Voice JS SDK** in the app's webview (WebRTC) | Audio goes laptop ↔ Twilio directly. No media server to run |
| Backend API | **Go on Vercel Functions** (Go runtime, `api/*.go`) | Free Hobby tier, git-push deploy |
| Database | **Neon** (serverless Postgres) | Free tier, `pgx` driver |
| Telephony | **Twilio trial** (MVP) → Indian licensed provider (prod) | See §6 |

The backend never carries audio. It only issues tokens, gives Twilio its call instructions, and logs calls.

## 2. Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────── Laptop ────────────────────────────┐
│  Wails app                                                     │
│   ├─ Go side: login, secure token storage (OS keychain)        │
│   └─ UI (React): dialer, call timer, history                   │
│        └─ Twilio Voice SDK ── WebRTC audio ──────────┐         │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┘
               │ HTTPS (JWT)                           │
┌──────────────▼──────────────┐                ┌───────▼────────┐
│  Vercel (Go functions)      │◄── webhooks ───│    Twilio      │
│   /api/login                │── TwiML ──────►│   (PSTN gw)    │
│   /api/token                │                └───────┬────────┘
│   /api/voice   (TwiML)      │                        │ PSTN
│   /api/status  (callback)   │                ┌───────▼────────┐
│   /api/calls   (history)    │                │ Indian mobile  │
└──────────────┬──────────────┘                │  +91XXXXXXXXXX │
               │ pgx (TLS)                     └────────────────┘
┌──────────────▼──────────────┐
│  Neon Postgres              │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

## 3. Call flow

```
App                  Vercel API              Twilio               Mobile
 │ POST /api/login ──►│ check bcrypt → JWT    │                     │
 │◄── JWT ────────────│                       │                     │
 │ GET /api/token ───►│ sign Access Token     │                     │
 │◄── twilio token ───│ (Voice grant, 1h TTL) │                     │
 │ Device.connect({To:"+91…"}) ─────────────► │                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/voice ───│ (signed webhook)    │
 │                    │ verify signature,     │                     │
 │                    │ validate +91 number,  │                     │
 │                    │ insert call row       │                     │
 │                    │── <Dial><Number> ────►│── ring ────────────►│
 │◄═════════════════ WebRTC audio ═══════════►│◄═══ voice ═════════►│
 │ hangup ───────────────────────────────────►│                     │
 │                    │◄── POST /api/status ──│ (duration, price)   │
 │                    │ update call row       │                     │
 │ GET /api/calls ───►│ history               │                     │
```

## 4. API

| Route | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/signup` | none | email + password → user (bcrypt) |
| `POST /api/login` | none | → app JWT (HS256, 7d) |
| `GET /api/token` | app JWT | → Twilio Access Token, identity = user id |
| `POST /api/voice` | Twilio signature | Returns TwiML `<Dial callerId=…><Number>+91…</Number></Dial>` |
| `POST /api/status` | Twilio signature | Final status, duration, price → `calls` |
| `GET /api/calls` | app JWT | User's last 50 calls |

Rules for `/api/voice`:
- Reject a request unless `X-Twilio-Signature` is valid. This stops strangers from using your account to place calls.
- `To` must match `^\+91[6-9]\d{9}$` (Indian mobile). Reject everything else so nobody can dial premium or international numbers.
- Per-user daily minute cap (MVP: 20 min), checked against `calls`.

## 5. Database (Neon)

```sql
create table users (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  email         text unique not null,
  password_hash text not null,
  created_at    timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table calls (
  id          uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid not null references users(id),
  call_sid    text unique not null,
  to_number   text not null,
  status      text not null default 'initiated',
  duration_s  int  not null default 0,
  price       numeric(10,4),
  created_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  ended_at    timestamptz
);
create index on calls (user_id, created_at desc);
```

## 6. India: provider and compliance

- **MVP (Twilio trial):** free trial credit. You can only call **verified** numbers (verify your test mobiles by OTP in the Twilio console). Every call starts with a trial announcement. Turn on India in *Voice → Geo Permissions*. Caller ID shows your Twilio number, which is not Indian. That's fine for testing.
- **Production:** under Indian telecom rules, internet-to-phone calling inside India must go through a licensed operator. Before launch, move to an Indian licensed cloud-telephony provider (e.g. Exotel, Plivo India, Airtel IQ, Tata Tele). These need business KYC. Keep all telephony code in `internal/telephony` so the switch only touches that package.
- Verify current rules with the provider during KYC. This section is not legal advice.

## 7. Repo layout

```
/
├── api/                  # Vercel Go functions (one Handler per file)
│   ├── login.go  signup.go  token.go  voice.go  status.go  calls.go
├── internal/
│   ├── db/               # pgx pool (Neon)
│   ├── auth/             # JWT + bcrypt
│   └── telephony/        # Twilio: token, TwiML, signature check
├── desktop/              # Wails app
│   ├── main.go  app.go   # Go side: login, keychain
│   └── frontend/         # React + TS + @twilio/voice-sdk
├── go.mod
└── DESIGN.md
```

## 8. Config (Vercel env vars)

```
DATABASE_URL            Neon pooled connection string
JWT_SECRET              random 32+ bytes
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN       used to verify webhooks
TWILIO_API_KEY_SID      used to sign access tokens
TWILIO_API_KEY_SECRET
TWILIO_TWIML_APP_SID    TwiML App → Voice URL = https://<app>.vercel.app/api/voice
TWILIO_CALLER_ID        your Twilio number
```

Secrets stay in Vercel only. The desktop app holds just the API base URL and the user's JWT, stored in the OS keychain.

## 9. Build order

0. **Spike (do first):** Wails app + Twilio SDK placing one call. This proves WebRTC and the microphone work in WebView2 (Windows) and WKWebView (macOS). The macOS build needs `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`. **If the mic or WebRTC fails in WKWebView, switch the desktop app to Electron.** The React UI carries over unchanged.
1. Neon schema + `internal/db`.
2. `signup` / `login` / `token`.
3. `voice` + `status` with signature checks, number validation, daily cap.
4. Desktop: login screen, dialer, call timer, history.
5. Package: `wails build` → `.exe` (Windows), `.app`/`.dmg` (macOS; signing and notarization needed for distribution).

## 10. Known limits

- Vercel Hobby is **non-commercial only**. Move to Pro before charging users.
- The Vercel Go runtime is the least mature Vercel runtime. Keep handlers plain `net/http` so they could move to any host.
- Twilio trial can only call verified numbers. Fine for an MVP with 10–20 test calls, not for real users.
- MVP skips: wallet/billing, contacts, call recording, incoming calls. Add once outbound works.

content.text:
I updated `DESIGN.md` so the laptop dialer has two modes you choose per call:
- **My phone (SIM):** the laptop sends the dial command and your Android phone places a normal SIM call. Free on an unlimited plan; you talk on the phone.
- **Internet (Twilio free trial):** you talk through the laptop's mic and speakers. Trial calls only reach numbers you've verified with Twilio.

The phone gets the dial command through Firebase push notifications, which are free.

Two things could break the plan, so we test them first:
- **Android:** does a phone in the background reliably place the call when the command arrives? Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones often kill background apps, so we test several brands.
- **Mac:** does the microphone work in the Go desktop app? If not, the desktop app switches to Electron and the screen code stays the same.

SIM mode only works with Android phones, since iPhones don't allow apps to place calls on their own. The phone app also has to be installed as a direct APK for now, because the Play Store limits access to the call log.

To start building I need a Firebase project (for the push notifications) and an Android phone to test on. Twilio and Neon can wait until the Twilio mode.

# Laptop Dialer

Dial from your laptop; your Android phone places the call on its SIM. Design: [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md).

## One-time setup

1. **Neon**: create a project, copy the *pooled* connection string, then
   `psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f db/schema.sql`
2. **Firebase**: create a project →
   - add an Android app with package `com.laptopdialer`, download `google-services.json` to `android/app/`
   - Project settings → Service accounts → *Generate new private key* (this JSON is `FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON`; never commit it)
3. **Env**: `cp .env.example .env` and fill it in (`openssl rand -base64 48` for `JWT_SECRET`).

## Run locally

```sh
set -a; source .env; set +a
go run ./cmd/dev                      # API on :8080
```

Android (phone on the same Wi‑Fi; use your laptop's LAN IP):
```sh
cd android && ./gradlew installDebug -PapiUrl=http://192.168.1.10:8080
```
Open the app → sign in → grant permissions → tap *Allow running in background*.

Desktop:
```sh
cd desktop && wails dev               # or: wails build -ldflags "-X main.apiURL=http://localhost:8080"
```

## Deploy API to Vercel

```sh
vercel link
vercel env add DATABASE_URL           # repeat for JWT_SECRET, FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON
vercel deploy --prod
```
Then rebuild the apps with `-PapiUrl=https://<app>.vercel.app` and `-X main.apiURL=https://<app>.vercel.app`.

## Test

```sh
go test ./... && (cd desktop && go test .)
```

content.text:
You don't need the rest of Firebase, only its push service (Firebase Cloud Messaging). Supabase can't stand in for it.

**Why push is needed:** Android stops background apps from holding their own network connections, especially in battery-saving mode and even more on Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones. The only connection Android keeps open in the background is Google Play Services', and Firebase push is what goes through it. That's why a dial command reaches the phone within a second, even when the helper app is closed.

**Why Supabase doesn't replace it:** Supabase Realtime is a live connection that the phone app has to keep open itself. To survive in the background it needs a permanent notification, it drains more battery, and those phone brands still cut it off. For mobile push, Supabase's own docs send notifications through Firebase anyway.

**Your options:**

| Option | Reliability | Cost | Extra work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Firebase push only (current)** | Best, wakes the phone instantly | Free | 10 min setup, already coded |
| Supabase Realtime or your own WebSocket | Medium. Needs an always-on notification, and some phone brands kill it | Free tier | Adds a second service next to Neon plus an always-on background service |
| ntfy / UnifiedPush (open source) | Medium, same background issue | Free | User installs a second app |
| Phone checks the server every few seconds | Poor, Android delays the checks by minutes | Free | Battery drain |

**Recommendation:** keep Firebase push. Your data, logins and call history stay on Neon. Firebase only carries a small "dial +91…" message, and it costs nothing.

If you'd rather avoid Google's service, the fallback is a live WebSocket connection with an always-on notification. Say so and I'll switch it, but expect missed calls on Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones.

content.text:
Cloudflare has the same problem as Supabase. The limit is on the phone, not the server.

- **What Cloudflare can do:** Durable Objects with WebSockets. Each phone keeps a live connection to Cloudflare, and the dial command goes straight to it. The free tier covers it, and it's the cleanest server for the WebSocket route.
- **What it can't do:** keep that connection alive on the phone. Android still closes the app's connection in the background, so you still need the always-on notification and still get missed calls on Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo phones. Cloudflare has no Android push service.

| Option | Server side | Phone side |
|---|---|---|
| **Firebase push (current)** | Free, already coded | Reliable, wakes the phone instantly |
| Cloudflare Durable Objects + WebSocket | Free, good | Always-on notification, can be killed |
| Supabase Realtime | Free tier | Always-on notification, can be killed |

Only Google Play Services is allowed to keep a connection open in the background on most Android phones, so any reliable option ends up using Firebase push.

**Recommendation:** keep Firebase push for dial commands. You could use Cloudflare later for something else, but not for waking the phone. If you still want to drop Firebase, I'd go with Cloudflare Durable Objects plus an always-on notification on the phone, accepting some missed calls. Which do you want?

content.text:
The laptop and the phone are separate devices. When you click **Call** on the laptop, something has to tell the phone "dial +91… now", and push is how that message gets there.

```
Laptop ──"dial +91…"──► Vercel ──push──► Phone ──SIM call──► person
```

**Why the server can't just contact the phone directly:**
- Your phone has no address the server can reach. Mobile networks and home Wi‑Fi hide it.
- When the screen is off, Android puts apps to sleep and cuts their connections.
- Push goes through Google Play Services, the one connection Android always keeps open, so it can wake the helper app within a second.

**It's not a notification you see.** It's a silent data message. The user sees nothing except the phone's normal call screen.

**Without push** you'd need one of these:
- the phone keeps its own connection to the server (always-on notification, killed by some phone brands), or
- the phone checks the server every few seconds (battery drain, Android delays it by minutes), or
- **a USB cable:** the laptop sends the dial command over USB debugging (`adb`). No server or helper app needed, but only for your own phone while it's plugged in or paired over Wi‑Fi debugging. Not suitable for other users.

For a product other people install, push is the right choice. If this is only for you right now, the USB route works today with no setup. Want me to add it as a quick test?

content.text:
**Why tell the phone:** in "My phone (SIM)" mode the laptop doesn't make the call. Your phone does, using its SIM card. The laptop has no SIM and can't reach the mobile network, so it acts as a remote dial pad: it tells your phone which number to call, and the phone dials.

```
Laptop (dial pad) ──► your phone (has SIM) ──normal call──► person
```

**What appears where:**

| Where | What's shown |
|---|---|
| The push message | Nothing visible. Hidden data: `{"type":"dial","call_id":"…","to":"[redacted]"}` |
| Your phone | Its normal outgoing call screen, plus a small notification: *"Call from laptop in progress"* (required by Android while the app watches the call) |
| The person you call | A normal incoming call from **your mobile number** |
| Laptop | "Calling from your phone. Talk on the phone." Then "Ended · 3:12" |

**If you don't want the phone involved,** that's the other mode, "Internet (Twilio)". The laptop calls directly and you talk through the laptop's mic and speakers. But the person sees a Twilio number, not yours, and it costs money after the trial.

Which mode did you have in mind? The phone dialing for you (shows your number, free), or the laptop calling on its own?

Then the call never happens. In SIM mode your phone is the only device that can place it: the laptop has no SIM card, can't reach the mobile network, and can't call a phone number on its own.

Without telling the phone, the only way to call is the **Internet (Twilio) mode**:

| | SIM mode (phone told) | Internet mode (phone not involved) |
|---|---|---|
| Who calls | Your phone | Twilio, from the laptop |
| Person sees | **Your number** | A Twilio number (not Indian on the trial) |
| Talk on | Phone | Laptop mic and speakers |
| Cost | Free (your plan) | Trial credit, then per minute |
| India rules | Normal mobile call, no issue | Needs a licensed Indian provider before real users |
| Needs Firebase | Yes | No |

There's no option where the laptop calls on its own, shows your mobile number, and costs nothing. Your number lives on your SIM, so the call has to come from the phone.
